summary.text: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System, a rocky world with only a trace atmosphere.
Its cratered surface resembles Earth's Moon, and its large core, rich in iron, fills about 57% of its volume.
With no atmosphere to trap heat, its equatorial regions swing from -170 °C at night to 420 °C in sunlight.

items.prompt: Mercury is closest to the Sun, yet Venus is hotter. What keeps Mercury cooler?

options.label: Its surface reflects nearly all sunlight
Thick clouds block most of the sunlight
It has no real atmosphere to hold heat in
It spins too fast to warm up

items.explain: Despite being closest to the Sun, Mercury is the second hottest because it lacks an atmosphere to trap heat.

items.prompt: A traveller on Mercury waits from one sunrise to the next. How long is that, compared with Mercury's year?

options.label: Twice as long
The same length
Half as long
A third as long

items.explain: One solar day lasts around 176 Earth days, twice Mercury's 88-day year.

items.prompt: Mercury is much smaller than Earth, yet nearly as dense. What does that say about its inside?

options.label: It has a thick mantle of ice
It has a hollow centre
It has a crust many hundreds of km deep
It has a large core that is rich in iron

items.explain: Its inner regions are less compressed, so such a high density means its core must be large and rich in iron.

items.prompt: Narrow ridges several hundred kilometres long cross Mercury's surface. How are they thought to have formed?

options.label: As water carved long channels across the crust
As its core and mantle cooled and shrank under a hardened crust
As giant ice sheets scraped across the land
As volcanoes poured out lines of lava

items.explain: The ridges are thought to come from the core and mantle cooling and contracting after the crust had already solidified.

items.prompt: Mercury's tilt is so small that crater floors near its poles never see the Sun. What might be sitting there?

options.label: Frozen water
Pools of liquid lava
Thick banks of cloud
Fields of loose sand

items.explain: Permanently shadowed poles strongly suggest water ice could be present in the craters.

items.prompt: Early Greeks saw a bright point at dawn and another at dusk. What did they come to realise?

options.label: They were two planets circling each other
One was a planet and the other a star
They were two separate planets of similar size
They were one and the same planet

items.explain: By about 350 BC the Greeks had realised the morning and evening 'stars' were the same body.

paragraphs.heading: Smallest and closest
paragraphs.text: Mercury is the planet nearest the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System. It is rocky, with only a trace of atmosphere and surface gravity a little lower than Mars has. As the innermost planet, it always shows up close to the Sun in our sky, either as a morning star or an evening star. In English it carries the name of Mercury, the Roman god of trade and communication and messenger of the gods.

paragraphs.heading: A Moon-like surface
paragraphs.text: Its surface looks a lot like our Moon's. It is cratered, crossed by a wide rupes system formed by thrust faults, and marked with bright rays of material thrown out by impacts. The largest crater, Caloris Planitia, is 1,550 km wide, about a third of the planet's 4,880 km diameter. Narrow ridges up to several hundred kilometers long also run across it. They probably formed as the core and mantle cooled and shrank after the crust had already hardened.

paragraphs.heading: Very long days
paragraphs.text: Mercury's year, 88.0 Earth days, and its sidereal day, 58.65 Earth days, are locked in a 3:2 ratio called a spin–orbit resonance. As a result, a full solar day, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about 176 Earth days, twice the length of its year. So one side stays in sunlight for a whole 88-day Mercurian year. On the next orbit, that same side sits in darkness for another 88 days until sunrise comes again.

paragraphs.heading: Fire and ice
paragraphs.text: Above the ground there is only an extremely thin exosphere. There is also a faint magnetic field, with barely enough strength to turn aside the solar wind. Combined with its highly eccentric orbit, this leaves the surface with wildly changing sunlight and temperature: at the equator, from −170 °C at night to 420 °C in sunlight. Even so, Mercury is only the second hottest planet, after Venus, because it has no atmosphere to trap heat. Its axis has very little tilt, so its poles are in permanent shadow, and that strongly suggests water ice could sit in craters there.

paragraphs.heading: A huge iron core
paragraphs.text: Mercury is roughly 70% metal and 30% silicate. At 5.427 g/cm³, its density is the second highest in the Solar System, just under Earth's. Earth's density comes partly from being squeezed by its own gravity, but Mercury is much smaller and less compressed inside. So for it to be this dense, its core must be large and rich in iron. That core fills about 57% of the planet's volume, against 17% for Earth.

paragraphs.heading: Layers, visitors and fate
paragraphs.text: Inside, Mercury seems to have a crust and mantle of solid silicate over a solid metal outer core, a liquid layer below that, and a solid inner core. It formed about 4.5 billion years ago, like the other planets. Mariner 10 made the first successful flyby in 1974, and the MESSENGER and BepiColombo orbiters have explored it since. In roughly seven or eight billion years, when the Sun becomes a red giant, Mercury is expected to be destroyed along with Venus.
